title: REST Principles
description: Understand the foundational principles of REST architecture and how they shape modern web API design. Learn about resources, statelessness, uniform interfaces, and how HTTP verbs map to operations.

blocks.text: REST stands for Representational State Transfer. It is an architectural style for building networked applications, not a strict standard or protocol. When someone says an API is "RESTful," they mean it follows a set of design principles that make it predictable, scalable, and easy to consume.

The core idea behind REST is that everything on the server is treated as a resource — a product, an order, a customer — and each resource has a unique identifier, usually a URL. Clients interact with these resources using standard HTTP methods, and the server responds with a representation of that resource, typically in JSON format.
What Makes an API RESTful?

Roy Fielding, who coined the term REST in his 2000 doctoral dissertation, defined six guiding constraints. An API does not need to satisfy all six to be called RESTful, but the more constraints it follows, the closer it is to true REST architecture.
Client-Server Separation

The client and server are independent. The client handles the user interface and user state, while the server handles data storage and business logic. This separation means you can update the mobile app without touching the backend, or scale the backend without changing the frontend.
Statelessness

Each request from the client must contain all the information the server needs to process it. The server must not store any client context between requests. This makes the API highly scalable because any server in a cluster can handle any request — there is no sticky session dependency.

blocks.title: Why Statelessness Matters
blocks.text: In a stateless API, a load balancer can route request #1 to Server A and request #2 to Server B with no issues. If the API were stateful and stored session data on a single server, scaling would require complex session-sharing mechanisms.
Uniform Interface

The interface between client and server must be consistent and standardized. REST achieves this through four sub-constraints: identification of resources, manipulation of resources through representations, self-descriptive messages, and hypermedia as the engine of application state (HATEOAS).
Resource Identification

Every resource is identified by a URI (Uniform Resource Identifier). For example, /api/products/42 identifies a single product. The URI should be a noun, not a verb. You would never see /api/getProduct/42 in a well-designed REST API.

blocks.title: Key REST Constraints at a Glance
items: Client-Server: Separate concerns between UI and data layers
Stateless: Every request is self-contained with no server-side session memory
Cacheable: Responses must define themselves as cacheable or non-cacheable
Uniform Interface: Standardized resource identification and manipulation
Layered System: Client cannot tell if it is connected to the end server or an intermediary
Code on Demand (optional): Server can extend client functionality by sending executable code

blocks.text: Resources and URIs

A REST API is organized around resources. A resource is any object, data, or service that can be accessed by the client. Resources are addressed using URIs, and the design of these URIs is one of the most visible aspects of API quality.

Good REST URIs use nouns to represent resources, follow a hierarchical structure for relationships, and use lowercase letters with hyphens for multi-word names. Plural nouns are the convention — /api/products, not /api/product.

blocks.title: Well-Designed Resource URIs
blocks.content: These URIs follow REST conventions — they use nouns, are hierarchical, and clearly identify the resource being addressed.
blocks.code:
GET    /api/products              # List all products
GET    /api/products/42            # Get product with ID 42
GET    /api/products/42/reviews    # Get reviews for product 42
POST   /api/products/42/reviews    # Create a new review for product 42
GET    /api/categories             # List all categories
GET    /api/categories/electronics # Get the electronics category

blocks.title: Avoid Verbs in URIs
blocks.text: URIs like /api/getProducts, /api/createOrder, or /api/deleteUser/5 are not RESTful. The HTTP method already tells the server what action to perform. Use nouns only.
HTTP Methods as Actions
In REST, the HTTP method (verb) tells the server what operation to perform on the resource identified by the URI. This is sometimes called the Uniform Interface constraint in action.

The most common HTTP methods in REST APIs are GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, and DELETE. Each method has a specific meaning, and using them consistently makes your API predictable for developers who consume it.

blocks.title: HTTP Methods Mapped to Resource Operations
blocks.content: A mapping of standard HTTP methods to CRUD operations on a Product resource.
blocks.code:
GET    /api/products          -> Retrieve all products (Read)
GET    /api/products/42        -> Retrieve product 42 (Read)
POST   /api/products           -> Create a new product (Create)
PUT    /api/products/42        -> Replace product 42 entirely (Update)
PATCH  /api/products/42        -> Update specific fields of product 42 (Update)
DELETE /api/products/42        -> Delete product 42 (Delete)

blocks.text: Representations

When a client requests a resource, the server does not send the internal database object. Instead, it sends a representation — usually a JSON document containing the resource's data. This representation is what the client sees and works with.

The same resource can have multiple representations. A product might be represented as JSON for a web API, XML for a legacy integration, or Protobuf for a high-performance mobile app. The client specifies the desired format using the Accept header.

blocks.title: JSON Representation of a Product Resource
blocks.content: When a client requests GET /api/products/42, the server returns this JSON representation.

terms.definition: Any object, data, or service accessible via the API, identified by a URI (e.g., /api/products/42).
The format in which a resource is delivered to the client, such as JSON or XML.
Each request contains all the information needed to process it; the server stores no client session state between requests.
Uniform Resource Identifier — the address used to locate a specific resource (e.g., /api/products).
An operation that produces the same result regardless of how many times it is called. GET, PUT, and DELETE are idempotent.

blocks.title: Design Tip: Think Nouns, Not Verbs
blocks.text: When designing your API URIs, always ask: 'What is this resource?' rather than 'What should I do with it?' The HTTP method answers the 'what to do' question. The URI answers 'what resource.'

blocks.title: Lesson Summary: REST Principles
points: REST is an architectural style, not a protocol — it provides guidelines rather than strict rules
Resources are identified by URIs and manipulated using standard HTTP methods
Statelessness means every request carries all context needed, enabling horizontal scaling
Good REST APIs use nouns in URIs and reserve HTTP methods for actions
Representations decouple the internal data model from what the client receives
REST constraints include client-server separation, caching, layered systems, and uniform interface
blocks.takeaway: REST gives you a shared language for designing APIs. When everyone uses the same conventions — GET for reading, POST for creating, nouns for resources — APIs become self-documenting and easier to integrate with.

blocks.title: Exercise: Design a RESTful URI Structure
blocks.description: Practice applying REST principles by designing a complete URI structure for a simple e-commerce API.
steps: Create a list of at least 5 resources for an online store (e.g., Products, Orders, Customers, Categories, Reviews)
Write the correct URI for listing all instances of each resource
Write the correct URI for retrieving a single item by ID from each resource
Write the correct URI for creating a new item in each resource using the proper HTTP method
Write URIs for nested resources (e.g., reviews for a specific product)
Identify any URIs that use verbs instead of nouns and rewrite them correctly
blocks.expectedOutcome: A clean URI map with only noun-based paths, correct HTTP method assignments, and properly nested sub-resources. Each URI should be immediately understandable by another developer without additional explanation.

items.text: I can explain what REST stands for and what it means for an API to be RESTful
items.hint: REST = Representational State Transfer. RESTful APIs follow design constraints for predictability.

items.text: I understand why URIs should use nouns, not verbs
items.hint: The HTTP method already defines the action. The URI should only identify the resource.

items.text: I can describe what statelessness means and why it is important for scalability
items.hint: Stateless means the server remembers nothing between requests — any server can handle any request.

items.text: I know the standard HTTP methods used in REST and what each one does
items.hint: GET (read), POST (create), PUT (replace), PATCH (partial update), DELETE (remove).

items.text: I can explain what a resource representation is and why it matters
items.hint: A representation is the format (usually JSON) sent to the client — it is a view of the resource, not the resource itself.
